metadata.title: It Flags and Ranks. It Never Convicts.
metadata.subtitle: The Fraud-Detection Skill (Medicare/Medicaid Claims Screening)
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when Claude screens a pile of Medicare/Medicaid claims for fraud, does it decide which providers committed fraud, or hand the finding to a person? Take the fraud-detection skill apart, explain the machinery — a folder Claude reads, a ranked and cited relay back out — and judge the design choice: pattern-matching at machine speed, judgment kept human.

beats.narration_text: Here's the wrong verb — thinking Claude convicts a Medicare claim of fraud. It doesn't. The fraud-detection skill screens the pile and hands the finding to a person. Does Claude flag fraudulent claims?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Does Claude convict fraudulent claims?', hesitates on 'convict', corrects to 'flag', lands the real question

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 1.0 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('convict' -> 'flag') lands on screen and the full corrected question finishes typing before the clip ends. Rates reused from the financial-services--claude-liam-kyc-rules sibling's proven working configuration (42ms/char, 8% hesitateBetween, 4% mistakeRate, short 4-line text). Teardown-register narration mirrors the on-screen correction: names the wrong verb, corrects it to what the skill actually does, restates the question with the corrected verb.

beats.narration_text: Here's what a skill actually is — a folder Claude reads before it works. No framework, no runtime, just files. The fraud-detection folder holds eight: a claims schema, reference data, a loader for the claims, a proposer for the detectors, an architecture doc, a package file, a README, and the SKILL.md itself. Claude reads them, then acts on what they say. The design bet is legibility — the file is the program, and a domain expert can audit every line.

Now the machinery. Claude points itself at the claims schema and the reference data, runs the claims through the proposed detectors, and relays one thing back: a ranked list of referrals. Each row names the provider by NPI, the suspected scheme, the dollar exposure, and a confidence score. They optimized for one output shape — a queue an investigator can work — at the cost of the exploratory tools a data analyst would want.

Here's what the whole thing is engineered for. Fraud-detection screens a Medicare/Medicaid claims corpus for fraud, waste, and abuse — and produces ranked, fully-cited referrals for an SIU or program-integrity team. Same input, same output, every run. That determinism is the point — an investigator can retrace exactly why a claim surfaced. What it sacrificed is autonomy: the skill never decides that fraud happened. It flags and ranks candidates. The investigation, and the finding, stay with a person.
Fraud-detection ranks and cites suspect claims for a person to investigate — it never decides that fraud happened.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt — paste it into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I have a batch of Medicare or Medicaid claims data and I want to screen it for possible fraud, waste, or abuse. Act as my first-pass screen, not the investigator: walk me through the schema and detectors you would load before you look at anything, show me the shape of the ranked, cited output you would relay back — provider NPI, suspected scheme, dollar exposure, confidence score — for each flag name the specific evidence a human reviewer can retrace, and tell me exactly where you stop and hand the determination to a person. Go deeper: what kinds of fraud would a rank-and-cite pipeline like this systematically miss, and what would it take to catch them without letting the model start deciding guilt? Liam, in for Bear.
